Could be true is not the same as must be true

Use small groups and counterexamples to separate a guaranteed conclusion from a tempting guess.

Start with exactly what you know

Suppose every amber token is round. You find an amber token. It must be round, because the rule covers every amber token.

Now suppose you find a round token. Must it be amber? No. The rule did not say that only amber tokens are round. A round blue token would fit the original rule too.

Try it yourself

Choose a statement about a tiny collection and test a conclusion. The activity shows a possible arrangement that fits the starting rule. Change the arrangement and look for a counterexample.

If one allowed arrangement makes a conclusion false, that conclusion is not guaranteed. It might still be possible. “Not guaranteed” is different from “impossible”.

+

Try it yourself

Look for a counterexample

Both arrangements obey the rule. Does the conclusion hold in both?

Some does not mean all

“Some round tokens are striped” tells you that at least one token is both round and striped. It does not tell you that every round token is striped. It also does not tell you how many plain round tokens exist.

Similarly, “all amber tokens are round” describes a relationship between groups. Without also saying an amber token exists, that sentence alone does not prove that the collection contains one. The examples in our activity make existence explicit.

Before the challenge

Read each condition, check the direction of the relationship, and separate what is guaranteed from what is merely compatible. A quick sketch of a few objects can expose a mistaken reversal.
